e: From Ancient Greek ξυστός (xustós, “smooth; scraped”), from ξύω (xúō, “scrape”), referring to its polished floor.
Learned borrowing from Latin xystarchēs, from Ancient Greek ξυστάρχης (xustárkhēs).

q: In a previous paper [Watt, 1930 ], I have reported the pharmacological effects of a glycoside, xysmalobin, isolated from the root by Brandwijk [1927].
1936, Watt, The South African Journal of Medical Sciences - Volumes 1-2, page 5:

Xysmalobium undulatum contains cardioactive steroid glycosides (cardenolides, mixture referred to as uzarone or xysmalobin): including among others uzarin (5.5%), xysmalorin (1.5%), allo-uzarine, allo-xysmalobin, urezin, uzaroside, ascleposide, and glucoascleposide.
2011, Amritpal Singh, Herbalism, Phytochemistry and Ethnopharmacology, page 129:

e: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ξυστόν (xustón, “spear, javelin”), of unknown origin. Potentially from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰasto- or *ǵʰasdʰo- (“branch ~ spear, sharp spine”) (whence also gad, goad, and yard), but this is likely a substrate word in view of the various irregularities.
q: The Companions, like the Thessalian cavalry, were a well-mounted force armed with cuirass and the short thrusting spear (xyston) for close combat.
2004, J. F. C. Fuller, The Generalship of Alexander the Great, page 47:

e: From Ancient Greek ξυστήρ (xustḗr, “scraper”), from ξύω (xúō, “scrape”).
